Ypsilandra thibetica forms tight rosettes of glossy, strap-shaped evergreen leaves from which upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers with prominent purple-black anthers emerge in late winter to early spring, well before most other woodland perennials break dormancy. A relative of Helonias and native to moist forests of the eastern Himalaya and southwestern China, it slowly forms a dense, weed-suppressing colony at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path, and its evergreen foliage and deer, rabbit, and slug resistance make it a useful year-round groundcover where hardy. Provide a steady mulch of leaf litter to buffer soil temperature and moisture, and avoid sites that bake in summer sun or dry out between waterings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; clumps spread gradually by rhizome into arching, bamboo-like stands and benefit from a spring topdressing of compost.

Disporum longistylum is a Chinese woodland perennial grown for its upright then gracefully arching stems clothed in narrow, evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves that emerge deep purple-black in early spring before maturing to green, with small, nodding, creamy white bell flowers appearing at the stem tips just as new growth unfurls. The widely grown selection 'Night Heron' is especially prized for its near-black spring stems and foliage and has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Site it where its architectural, cane-like stems can be appreciated against a dark backdrop in a shaded border, and divide congested clumps in early spring if flowering declines.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in rich, humusy, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give regular water through summer to keep the glossy evergreen foliage from scorching, and cut back old flower spikes in late summer.

Beesia deltophylla is a Chinese woodland evergreen forming a slowly spreading clump of glossy, deltoid, heart-shaped leaves that emerge with a distinct bronze cast before deepening to rich glossy green, topped in mid to late spring by slender spires of small white flowers held well above the foliage. Its lustrous, weather-resistant leaves make it a handsome year-round groundcover or path edging in a shaded garden, pairing well with hellebores, hardy ferns, and other Asian woodland perennials that share its preference for humus-rich, evenly moist soil. It is deer resistant and largely untroubled by pests, needing only an annual mulch and division every several years once clumps become congested.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; arching stems emerge from creeping rhizomes and clumps expand steadily without becoming invasive, tolerating average garden soil once established.

Polygonatum falcatum is a Japanese woodland species producing gracefully arching stems lined with paired, glossy, pointed leaves and hung in late spring with small, cream, green-tipped, bell-shaped flowers dangling in pairs or trios along the underside of the stem. It is the parent of several popular variegated selections such as 'Nippon Sunbeam' and 'Silver Lining', but the green species itself makes a refined textural addition to a shaded border or woodland garden, contrasting well with broad-leaved hostas and ferns. Established clumps need little care beyond a yearly mulch of leaf compost and division every four to five years to maintain vigor.

Vancouveria hexandra is a deciduous native of moist coastal and montane forests from Washington through northern California, forming loose colonies of wiry, dark stems bearing delicate, apple-green leaves divided into small heart-shaped leaflets, with airy clusters of tiny white flowers held above the foliage on thread-like stalks in late spring. Its common name refers to the reflexed, backward-swept petals that give each miniature flower an inside-out appearance, and its finely divided foliage adds fine texture beneath native shrubs and conifers where it functions as a well-mannered, non-aggressive groundcover. Unlike its evergreen relative Vancouveria planipetala, this species dies back in winter, so leave the previous year's dried foliage in place until new growth resumes in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring directly into saturated, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along a streambank, seep, or bog garden; this tiny native mat-former needs constantly wet soil and will not persist in average garden conditions.

Chrysosplenium americanum is a diminutive eastern North American wildflower found carpeting shaded seeps, spring runs, and streamside mud from the Great Lakes and Northeast south through the Appalachian Mountains, forming loose, creeping mats of small, rounded, opposite leaves studded in early spring with inconspicuous but ecologically valuable yellow-green flowers that draw small early-season pollinators. It naturalizes readily in a shaded bog garden, rain garden margin, or the muddy edge of a garden pond, filling gaps between sedges and ferns where few other groundcovers will grow in standing wet soil. Because it spreads by shallow, brittle stems that root as they creep, established patches are easily divided and moved in spring to extend the planting along a wet shaded edge.
